title: /add-coverage command
content:
Find a coverage gap, write a test, validate it catches regressions, review it, commit, and open a PR.
/dotnet-testing:add-coverage # target the whole solution /dotnet-testing:add-coverage Acme.Store.Api # target a namespace /dotnet-testing:add-coverage PaymentService # target a class The pipeline Phase Runs as Output 0. Ensure environment orchestrator Verifies CLI tools, local tools, coverage.runsettings, and test-project packages — offers to fix gaps, only with your approval 1. Find the gap coverage-gap-finder agent gap-report.md — exactly one highest-CRAP untested method 2. Write the test test-author agent One new xUnit test file, passing green 3. Validate it has teeth mutation-validator agent mutation-result.md — PASS/FAIL via Stryker or a manual mutation 4. Review quality test-reviewer agent review-notes.md — LGTM or numbered refactor requests 5. Commit orchestrator Branch test/add-coverage-{ClassName} pushed 6. Open PR orchestrator PR describing the gap, the test, and the mutation evidence If the reviewer requests changes, test-author is re-invoked once as a refactor pass and the review repeats; if the second review still has issues, the pipeline stops and reports rather than looping. It also stops (and tells you why) if the build is broken, no meaningful gap exists, or the mutation validation fails.
How the agents hand off Agents share no conversation context. They communicate through files in .claude/add-coverage-work/, created at the start of a run and deleted after the PR opens:
File Written by Read by gap-report.md coverage-gap-finder test-author, mutation-validator new-test-path.txt test-author mutation-validator, test-reviewer mutation-result.md mutation-validator orchestrator (PR body) review-notes.md test-reviewer test-author (refactor pass) The isolation is deliberate: test-reviewer receives only the test file path, so its review is not anchored by the pipeline’s reasoning.
Two files are meant to persist in your repo (created only with approval, never overwritten): coverage.runsettings and .config/dotnet-tools.json.
What each phase leans on Phase 1 applies the crap-analysis skill’s scoring and exclusion rules. Phase 2 picks a test type per test-type-selection and follows test-authoring conventions exactly. Phase 3 follows stryker-dotnet, falling back to one manual mutation when Stryker isn’t installed. Phase 4 reviews against the same two convention skills Phase 2 wrote under.
Troubleshooting “No meaningful gap was found” — all methods have CRAP < 30 and coverage > 80%. Narrow with a namespace argument, or celebrate. Mutation validator FAIL — the test doesn’t assert the right observable outcome; the report names the surviving mutation and what assertion would catch it. Build broken — Phase 1 stops immediately if dotnet build fails. Fix the build first. gh not authenticated — run gh auth login; the pipeline can still run through commit without it. Stryker not found — the validator falls back to a manual mutation; add dotnet-stryker to .config/dotnet-tools.json to use Stryker.
description: The six-phase pipeline that orchestrates the plugin’s four agents

title: adr-writing
content:
Write Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for a project’s documentation. Covers file naming, frontmatter, required sections, status lifecycle, index maintenance, and detecting/fixing duplicate ADR numbers from parallel branches. Load before creating, revising, or superseding any ADR, or when asked to check for duplicate ADR numbers or fix the ADR list.
Invoke with /architecture:adr "<decision-description>" or /architecture:adr --issue <N>.
What it covers The full authoring workflow, with one meta-rule above all: existing repository conventions win over this skill — read a few recent ADRs first and match their style.
Locating and numbering — find the repo’s ADR directory, then derive the next number from index titles and title: frontmatter rather than filenames (filenames drift; renaming changes published URLs). Files are adr-NNN-short-slug.md. Required sections — Context, Problem Statement, Decision, Options Considered (each option either (chosen) or with a codebase-verified Rejected because:), Rationale, Consequences split Positive/Negative, Open Issues, Future Considerations, Related Links. The skill insists on honest negatives: “an ADR with no negatives reads as unexamined.” Status lifecycle — Proposed → Active → Superseded, handled append-only: never delete or renumber old ADRs; link the old status line to the successor. Duplicate numbers from parallel branches — a detection-and-resolution procedure: the first-merged ADR keeps the number, the later one is renumbered to highest+1 (never filling gaps) in a single atomic commit that updates the file, the index, and every repo-wide reference. Ships with File Contents template.md A blank ADR skeleton with prompts for every section examples/full-example-adr.md A complete worked ADR — the reference for tone and rigor examples/superseded-example-adr.md Demonstrates the superseded status line examples/example-index.md A sample ADR index page Cross-references Standalone — references no other skills or agents, though the technical-writer agent in this plugin covers ADRs among the document types it produces. Uses gh pr list and git log when resolving duplicate numbers across branches. This repository’s own devdocs/ADRs follow this skill’s format.
description: The full ADR authoring workflow

title: csharp-coding-standards
content:
Write modern, high-performance C# code using records, pattern matching, value objects, async/await, Span<T>/Memory<T>, and best-practice API design patterns. Emphasizes functional-style programming with C# 12+ features.
What it covers The house C# style, built on a set of core principles:
Immutability by default — record types and init setters; value objects are readonly record struct, never classes, and never define implicit conversion operators. Pattern matching over branching — switch expressions preferred to if/else chains. Async everywhere — every async method takes a CancellationToken; libraries use ConfigureAwait(false); no blocking on async code. Composition over inheritance — interfaces plus composition instead of abstract base classes. No reflection-based mapping — AutoMapper, Mapster, and ExpressMapper are explicitly banned in favor of hand-written mapping extension methods, with UnsafeAccessorAttribute (.NET 8+) as the escape hatch for private access. Errors split two ways — Result<T, TError> for expected business failures; exceptions only for unexpected/system errors. Performance-aware APIs — Span<T>, Memory<T>, and ArrayPool<T> on hot paths; accept abstractions, return appropriately specific types. Ships with The SKILL.md is a hub; detail lives in four supporting files Claude loads only when relevant:
File Contents value-objects-and-patterns.md readonly record struct value objects, TypeConverter for config binding, full C# 8–12 pattern-matching examples performance-and-api-design.md Zero-allocation Span<T>/Memory<T> code and method-signature design composition-and-error-handling.md Inheritance-to-composition refactors and the full Result<T, TError> implementation anti-patterns-and-reflection.md Why reflection mapping is banned, explicit mapping methods, and eight named anti-patterns Cross-references Standalone — it references no other skills or agents. The dotnet-agent in this plugin follows the same conventions when implementing features, and the test-authoring skill in dotnet-testing applies the same spirit to test code.
description: The NimblePros C# house style

title: feature-specification
content:
Generates a structured feature specification markdown file from a GitHub issue. Use when creating a spec for a new feature, epic, or backlog item that needs implementation planning.
What it covers The exact shape of a spec file written to .claude/specs/<issue-number>-<short-title>.md:
A header block — title, **GitHub Issue**: #<number>, status, Overview, Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope, Open Questions. Sequential implementation phases, each with a Goal, a - [ ] task checklist, Details, and objectively verifiable “Done When” exit conditions — subjective criteria are explicitly banned. Each phase header names the agent or role that executes it, falling back to a plain role (“backend”, “UI”) when the project has no matching agent. Opinionated phase ordering: data layer → API layer → UI layer → tests. Every API endpoint gets example request/response JSON; ambiguity means asking clarifying questions, not assuming. Cross-references This is the document format the spec-agent delegates to — the agent decides when to write a spec; this skill defines what one looks like. Downstream, the pr-agent verifies the spec’s acceptance criteria before opening a PR. The sibling implement-feature skill uses a similar phased structure but writes plans to .claude/plans/ instead. Not slash-invocable; no supporting files.
description: Specs a developer can implement without asking questions

title: playwright-issue-repro-report
content:
Reproduce GitHub issues with Playwright, collect screenshot/video/trace artifacts, and publish evidence-based issue comments. Use when a bug report needs reproducible UI steps and supporting artifacts for triage.
What it covers Turning a narrative bug report into a deterministic, evidence-backed triage artifact:
Extract expected vs. observed behaviour and preconditions from the issue. Draft or adapt a Playwright test using semantic locators and user-visible assertions — no hard sleeps, no implementation-detail assertions. Run it, collecting failure.png, trace.zip, and video artifacts. Publish a ready-to-post GitHub comment stating repro status, environment, exact steps, and artifact links. Its guardrails are the point: never claim reproduction unless the assertion and the artifacts agree; always classify the outcome as reproduced, not reproduced, or inconclusive; never include secrets in issue comments.
Ships with File Contents references/WORKFLOW.md The seven-step operational reference from gathering issue context through posting the comment and deciding next action templates/issue-repro-prompt.md Fill-in-the-blank prompt for kicking off a repro session templates/issue-comment-template.md The comment skeleton: repro status, environment, steps, observed vs. expected, evidence, notes Cross-references Requires Playwright and posts comments via the gh CLI (or manual upload in the GitHub web UI). The worked examples in the supporting files are .NET-flavored (dotnet test, a C# Playwright project) even though the workflow itself is stack-neutral — adapt the commands to your stack. It references no other skills or agents; the e2e-tester agent in this plugin is its natural companion for maintaining the broader e2e suite.
description: From narrative bug report to deterministic repro with artifacts

title: playwright-design-review
content:
Compare a design asset (image or PDF) against live screenshots of the implementation captured by Playwright. Detects visual differences, prioritizes them by user impact, suggests corrections, and optionally creates one GitHub issue per finding.
What it covers A structured design-QA pass that produces a human-reviewable audit trail:
Accept a reference design as an image (.png, .jpg, .webp) or PDF. PDFs are split per-page using pdftoppm or PyMuPDF before comparison. Capture full-page Playwright screenshots of the live implementation at the specified viewport. Pixel-diff each pair, annotate a diff overlay, and crop evidence images per region. Classify every difference by severity and output a prioritized findings list. Suggest a concrete, actionable correction per finding. Optionally create one GitHub issue per finding using the gh CLI. The guardrails matter: findings are never escalated to design:critical on subjective grounds alone — functional or accessibility impact is required. Ambiguous or dynamic regions are always classified as design:info rather than guessed.
Severity model Label Criteria design:critical Core layout broken, content obscured, inaccessible element design:high Wrong component used, wrong brand color or typography affecting readability design:medium Spacing off by more than 8px, missing icon, text truncation design:low Minor shade variation, pixel-level shadow, icon size ±2px design:info Ambiguous region, dynamic content, responsive variant out of scope Ships with File Contents references/PDF_EXTRACTION.md Steps for extracting PDF pages as PNG using pdftoppm and PyMuPDF templates/findings-report.md Prioritized findings report with summary table, per-finding evidence, and inconclusive regions templates/github-issue-template.md GitHub issue body with evidence table, bounding-box location, suggested correction, and acceptance criteria Invoke via command The /playwright-testing:design-review command runs the full pipeline end-to-end from a single invocation: PDF extraction, Playwright screenshot capture, visual diff, report generation, and optional GitHub issue creation.
Cross-references Pairs with playwright-issue-repro-report — that skill produces evidence from an existing bug report; this skill generates the findings before bugs are reported. Issue creation uses the same gh CLI flow as the repro-report skill.
description: From mockup to implementation gap list, with optional GitHub issue creation

title: crap-analysis
content:
Analyze code coverage and CRAP (Change Risk Anti-Patterns) scores to identify high-risk code. Use OpenCover format with ReportGenerator for Risk Hotspots showing cyclomatic complexity and untested code paths.
Invoke standalone with /dotnet-testing:crap-analysis [project-or-namespace-filter].
What it covers The CRAP formula — comp(m)² × (1 − cov(m)/100)³ + comp(m) — and how to read it: under 5 is low risk, 5–30 medium, over 30 means the method needs tests or refactoring. A key insight the skill demonstrates with a worked example: a complexity-80 method scores 80 even at 100% coverage — CRAP flags complexity that coverage alone can’t fix.
Practically, it provides:
A complete coverage.runsettings — OpenCover format is mandatory (cobertura carries no complexity metrics) — with the exclusion set for test/benchmark/migration assemblies and generated code. ReportGenerator setup as a pinned local tool, the collect → report command sequence, and how to read the Risk Hotspots table. Recommended thresholds: line > 80%, branch > 60%, CRAP < 30 for new code (relaxed to 60/40 for legacy) — and the firm opinion that thresholds are never lowered because code is “too hard to test”; you refactor instead. Cross-references This skill is the knowledge behind Phase 1 of /add-coverage — the coverage-gap-finder agent loads it, and the command’s environment check uses it as the source of truth for coverage.runsettings and the ReportGenerator tool entry. External tools: dotnet test with coverlet, and dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool. Single-file skill.
description: Change Risk Anti-Patterns via OpenCover + ReportGenerator

title: Getting Started
content:
Add the marketplace once, then install only the plugins you want.
Option A — Claude Code plugin install (recommended) claude plugin marketplace add NimblePros/claude-plugins claude plugin install <plugin>@nimblepros This installs that plugin’s commands, agents, and skills into your global Claude Code configuration so they are available in every project. Available plugin names: dotnet, dotnet-testing, testing, architecture, workflow.
Option B — Per-project install via .claude/settings.json Add the marketplace and the plugins you want to your project’s .claude/settings.json so all collaborators get them when they trust the folder:
{ "extraKnownMarketplaces": { "nimblepros": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "NimblePros/claude-plugins" } } }, "enabledPlugins": { "dotnet-testing@nimblepros": true, "workflow@nimblepros": true } } Option C — Manual copy (standalone, no marketplace) Copy a single plugin’s contents into your project’s .claude/ directory. Skills and commands are then available without namespacing (/add-coverage instead of /dotnet-testing:add-coverage):
# From your project root gh repo clone NimblePros/claude-plugins /tmp/nimblepros-plugins mkdir -p .claude cp -r /tmp/nimblepros-plugins/plugins/dotnet-testing/commands .claude/ cp -r /tmp/nimblepros-plugins/plugins/dotnet-testing/agents .claude/ cp -r /tmp/nimblepros-plugins/plugins/dotnet-testing/skills .claude/ Commit the .claude/ directory so the whole team gets it.
Command namespacing When installed as a plugin (Options A and B), commands and skills are namespaced by the plugin name:
/dotnet-testing:add-coverage [optional: namespace or class name] /workflow:review /workflow:commit When installed via Option C (standalone copy into .claude/), use the short form (/add-coverage, /review, /commit).
Requirements Requirements vary per plugin — each plugin page lists its own. In general:
git and gh (GitHub CLI, authenticated via gh auth login) for workflow and the /dotnet-testing:add-coverage pipeline the .NET SDK plus test tooling for dotnet-testing nothing beyond Claude Code itself for the knowledge-only skills Migrating from the single nimblepros plugin This repository previously published one plugin containing everything, installed as nimblepros@nimblepros. That plugin no longer exists. Claude Code v2.1.193 and later migrate automatically — the marketplace records the removal, so the stale entry is dropped from your settings with a one-line notice. On earlier versions, or to pick your replacements explicitly:
claude plugin uninstall nimblepros@nimblepros claude plugin marketplace update nimblepros claude plugin install dotnet-testing@nimblepros # plus any others you want /nimblepros:add-coverage is now /dotnet-testing:add-coverage. The marketplace name is unchanged, so the marketplace itself does not need to be re-added.
description: Three installation options, command namespacing, and migration from the old single plugin

title: implement-feature
content:
End-to-end workflow for implementing, fixing, or otherwise working on a specific GitHub issue. Fetches full issue context with the gh CLI, produces a phased implementation plan in .claude/plans, implements it, gets an independent agent review, verifies build/tests/format, and opens a pull request that references the issue. Use whenever asked to implement, fix, or work on a GitHub issue by number or URL.
Invoke with /workflow:implement <issue-number-or-url>.
What it covers The plugin’s flagship seven-step loop:
Gather context exhaustively — gh issue view with all fields, read every comment, download referenced screenshots and attachments (they “frequently contain the actual acceptance criteria”), follow every linked issue and PR. Plan before code — persist a phased plan at .claude/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-issue-NNN-slug.md before writing anything. Resuming an issue that already has a plan skips straight to implementation. Implement on a feature branch — never main; write the tests the plan calls for. Independent review — launch a separate review agent with fresh context and address all significant findings. Final verification — build, tests, formatting all clean. Open the PR — gh pr create with Fixes #NNN / Closes #NNN (or Relates to #NNN for partial work). Summarize — plan path, branch, PR URL, and any deferred work. Its guardrails are worth quoting: “Never skip, weaken, or disable tests to get to green” and “Report failures honestly.”
Cross-references Step 4’s independent review is exactly what the review skill provides. The plan format parallels feature-specification (but plans live in .claude/plans/, specs in .claude/specs/). The skill directs Claude to load any relevant domain skills during implementation — e.g. test-authoring from dotnet-testing on a .NET project. Its verification examples reference a .NET build/format harness; substitute your own stack’s equivalent. Requires git and an authenticated gh. Also triggers whenever you ask Claude to implement or fix an issue by number or URL without the slash command.
description: Issue in, reviewed PR out

title: package-management
content:
Manage NuGet packages using Central Package Management (CPM) and dotnet CLI commands. Never edit XML directly - use dotnet add/remove/list commands. Use shared version variables for related packages.
What it covers The golden rule: package changes go through the dotnet CLI (dotnet add/remove/list package), never through hand-edited .csproj or Directory.Packages.props — the CLI validates the package exists, resolves versions, and handles transitive dependencies.
On top of that:
Central Package Management setup — ManagePackageVersionsCentrally with versionless PackageReference entries. Shared version variables — MSBuild properties like $(AspireVersion) or $(OpenTelemetryVersion) keep families of related packages in lockstep. When not to use CPM — legacy solutions, version ranges (unsupported), older tooling (needs SDK 6.0.300+, NuGet 6.2+, VS 2022 17.2+). Troubleshooting (cache clearing, transitive trees, lock files), private feed / NuGet.config setup, and a quick-reference command table. Cross-references The skill flags VersionOverride as something the NimblePros Slopwatch tooling detects as potential slop — that check lives outside this marketplace. Optional companion tooling: dotnet-outdated-tool for bulk upgrades. Single-file skill; no supporting files.
description: Never hand-edit package XML

title: /repro-issue command
content:
Reproduce a GitHub issue with Playwright, collect screenshot/video/trace artifacts, and publish evidence-based issue comments.
/playwright-testing:repro-issue 42 # by issue number /playwright-testing:repro-issue https://github.com/org/repo/issues/42 The pipeline Phase What happens 0. Prerequisites Verifies dotnet, git, gh auth; installs Playwright Chromium if needed 1. Fetch issue gh issue view — extracts expected behaviour, observed behaviour, and preconditions 2. Build repro Drafts or adapts a Playwright C# test using semantic locators and user-visible assertions 3. Run and collect Runs a targeted test filter; collects failure.png, trace.zip, and video from TestResults/PlaywrightArtifacts/ 4. Post comment Populates and posts the issue comment template; falls back to printing if gh auth is unavailable Repro status The command always declares one of three outcomes — it never posts ambiguous commentary:
Reproduced — test failed with the same observable symptom as the issue. Not Reproduced — test passed; what was checked is documented. Inconclusive — test errored for unrelated reasons or environment could not be verified. What it leans on Built on the playwright-issue-repro-report skill. The comment it posts follows templates/issue-comment-template.md from that skill; the Playwright test conventions follow the same semantic-locator priority as the broader testing practice.
Handoff files File Written by .claude/repro-work/issue-context.md Phase 1 — issue title, expected/observed, preconditions .claude/repro-work/repro-test-path.txt Phase 2 — path to the repro test file .claude/repro-work/artifacts.md Phase 3 — paths to screenshot, trace, and video .claude/repro-work/issue-comment.md Phase 4 — ready-to-post comment body The .claude/repro-work/ directory is intentionally left after the run as an audit trail.
description: From issue number to posted evidence comment in four automated phases

title: commit
content:
Generate a commit message following project conventions. Use when the user says “commit”, “commit this”, “make a commit”, or invokes /commit.
Invoke with /workflow:commit.
What it covers A three-step commit flow:
Confirm intent — work item ID (auto-detected from the branch name where possible) and commit type (fix, feat, refactor, chore, docs, test, perf), asked only when the conversation doesn’t already make both obvious. Gather evidence — git status, git diff -w HEAD, recent log. Notable opinion: derive the message from conversation context first, falling back to the diff — the conversation knows why, the diff only knows what. Confirm and commit — present the message for approval, then stage and commit. A hard rule: never amend a previous commit without explicit approval. Ships with File Contents references/conventions.md The full Conventional Commits v1.0.0 reference: type-to-SemVer table, breaking-change syntax, and an anti-patterns list (no file lists, no subject restatement, no “This commit…”) Cross-references references/conventions.md is the most complete of the plugin’s three Conventional Commits sources — the conventional-commit skill covers the same spec as a prompt template, and the pr skill applies the same title format to pull requests. Uses git only (no gh).
description: /workflow:commit — conversation-aware Conventional Commits

title: dotnet
content:
C# and .NET practice — how NimblePros writes, configures, and ships .NET code.
claude plugin install dotnet@nimblepros This plugin is pure knowledge and agents: five skills and two agents, no slash commands. The skills are reference material Claude loads on demand while writing .NET code; you don’t invoke them directly.
Skills Skill One-line summary csharp-coding-standards Modern C# 12+: records, pattern matching, value objects, Span<T>, and a hard ban on reflection-based mappers package-management Central Package Management driven entirely through the dotnet CLI — never hand-edit package XML microsoft-extensions-configuration The Options pattern with validation on startup microsoft-extensions-dependency-injection Composable IServiceCollection extension methods instead of a 200-line Program.cs opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation Resilient, low-overhead tracing and metrics with ActivitySource and Meter The configuration and dependency-injection skills cross-reference each other — DI extension methods are where options registration lives, and the DI skill points at the configuration skill for the Options pattern.
Agents dotnet-agent implements server-side features in C#/.NET/ASP.NET Core/EF Core from an approved specification: it reads the spec from specs/ before writing code, works test-first with xUnit, and updates the spec as it completes work. It pairs naturally with the workflow plugin’s spec-producing agents, though neither plugin requires the other.
publish-nuget runs a gated NuGet release pipeline: pre-publish checklist (SemVer, release notes, metadata, zero-warning build, passing tests), then version bump → RELEASE_NOTES.md entry → pack → inspect → push → git tag. It reads the API key from the NUGET_API_KEY environment variable and never publishes from a dirty working tree. Note: its example paths target the Nimble.Endpoints package — point it at your own .csproj when using it elsewhere.
Requirements The skills need nothing beyond Claude Code. The agents use the dotnet CLI, and publish-nuget additionally needs git and a NUGET_API_KEY environment variable.
Related plugins .NET testing deliberately lives in dotnet-testing — coverage analysis, mutation testing, and xUnit conventions.
description: How NimblePros writes, configures, and ships .NET code

title: microsoft-extensions-configuration
content:
Microsoft.Extensions.Options patterns including IValidateOptions, strongly-typed settings, validation on startup, and the Options pattern for clean configuration management.
What it covers Configuration as a fail-fast discipline: bind settings to POCOs with a public const string SectionName, then .BindConfiguration(...).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() — with .ValidateOnStart() called out as the critical, frequently-forgotten piece (without it, validation is deferred to first access).
Data Annotations vs. IValidateOptions<T> — a clear dividing line: annotations for simple required/range rules, a validator class for cross-property, conditional, or DI-dependent checks. Lifetime selection — when to use IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, or IOptionsMonitor<T> (including OnChange in a BackgroundService). Anti-patterns — injecting raw IConfiguration, validating in constructors, omitting ValidateOnStart, and throwing instead of returning ValidateOptionsResult.Fail from a validator. Ships with File Contents advanced-patterns.md Validators with constructor dependencies, named options, a complete production validator example, and unit-testing configuration validators Cross-references Referenced by microsoft-extensions-dependency-injection for the Options pattern — registration of validated options typically lives inside the DI extension methods that skill prescribes.
description: Fail fast on bad configuration

title: test-authoring
content:
Conventions for writing xUnit tests. Covers naming, assertion style (Shouldly), mocking (NSubstitute), fixture patterns, and the rules that make tests meaningful vs. ornamental. Load this skill before writing or reviewing any test file.
What it covers Naming — test classes <Subject>_<Scenario> (a separate class per distinct outcome), methods <ExpectedOutcome>_<Condition>. Structure — Arrange-Act-Assert inline, no constructor setup, one behaviour per test, one class per file. Assertions and mocking — Shouldly over bare Assert.*; NSubstitute over Moq or hand-rolled fakes. Fixtures — file static class fixtures with a Make() factory carrying sensible defaults. The most important rule — “a test that passes when the code is broken is worse than no test.” The acceptance question: would deleting the key source line make this test fail? Good assertion targets (return values, public state, .Received() calls) vs. bad ones (private fields, framework behaviour, tautologies). Placement ladder — alongside existing tests for the class → the project with the <ProjectReference> → naming convention → stop and ask rather than guess. Cross-references Tells the reader to load test-type-selection first to decide what kind of test to write. Both the test-author and test-reviewer agents in the /add-coverage pipeline load it — the reviewer’s checklist cites this skill’s sections by name, and reviewers are forbidden from raising stylistic preferences not found in it. If your stack uses NUnit, FluentAssertions, or Moq instead, fork the repo and edit this skill — it is the single place the framework conventions live.
description: The house style for .NET tests

title: /refactor-tests command
content:
Refactor generated or messy Playwright .NET test files into clean, maintainable xUnit tests with role-based locators and intent-based assertions.
/playwright-testing:refactor-tests tests/E2E/LoginTests.cs /playwright-testing:refactor-tests "tests/E2E/**/*Tests.cs" # omit argument to auto-discover all Playwright test files in the workspace The pipeline Phase What happens 0. Prerequisites Verifies dotnet; resolves $ARGUMENTS to a list of Playwright C# test files 1. Baseline run Builds and runs the targets to confirm their current green state; stops (with permission) if any are already red 2. Refactor each file Applies the six refactor rules (see below); writes improvements back to disk; logs a one-line change summary per file 3. Verify green Re-runs the same tests; reverts any file that becomes newly red and adds it to a manual-review list 4. Report Prints a summary: files refactored, key improvements, files skipped or reverted Refactor rules Preserve user intent — no silently added or removed scenario steps. Upgrade locators: GetByRole → GetByLabel/GetByPlaceholder → GetByText → GetByTestId; CSS/XPath only as last resort. Write readable xUnit — obvious Arrange-Act-Assert, intent-revealing test names. Extract helpers only when readability genuinely improves. Assert only user-observable behaviour — never internal IDs, CSS class internals, or hidden DOM. Deterministic waits via Playwright assertions — no await Task.Delay. What it leans on Built on the playwright-dotnet-refactor skill. That skill defines the rules, the output contract, and the rationale format. This command applies them in batch over a file or glob, wraps the run with a green-gate, and surfaces a summary rather than inline reasoning.
Handoff files File Contents .claude/refactor-work/baseline.txt Pass/fail counts before refactoring .claude/refactor-work/changes.md One-line change log per file, plus any assumptions
description: Batch-refactor codegen noise into maintainable xUnit tests

title: conventional-commit
content:
Reference material for the Conventional Commits format used across the workflow plugin. Not an installable skill — loaded by the commit skill and cited by pr-agent and the pr skill for PR title format requirements.
What it covers A reference page (not an installable skill): a structured scaffold for building a commit message — type, optional scope, imperative-mood description, body, footer — plus examples and validation rules (type must come from the allowed set; description is required). It explicitly notes that the same <type>: <description> structure doubles as the PR title format, which is why the PR-facing pieces of this plugin point back here.
Cross-references The pr-agent cites this skill by name for its draft-PR title format, and the pr skill enforces the same conventional title (with a 65-character cap). It overlaps heavily with the fuller reference in commit’s references/conventions.md — when in doubt, treat that file as canonical for message content and this skill as the quick template. Not slash-invocable; no supporting files; uses plain git.
description: The structured format behind commits and PR titles

title: dotnet-testing
content:
The .NET testing toolkit, built around a single command that finds the highest-risk untested method, writes a mutation-validated xUnit test, reviews it for quality, commits, and opens a PR.
claude plugin install dotnet-testing@nimblepros This plugin is deliberately .NET-specific — it depends on dotnet test, ReportGenerator, Stryker.NET, xUnit, Shouldly, and NSubstitute. For stack-neutral testing practice, see the testing plugin.
Commands Command One-line summary /dotnet-testing:add-coverage Six-phase pipeline: find the highest-CRAP gap → write test → validate it has teeth → review → commit → open PR /dotnet-testing:crap-analysis Collect coverage, generate a CRAP score report, surface the top risk hotspots /dotnet-testing:mutation-test Run Stryker.NET against a source file or class, report killed vs. survived mutations Skills Skill One-line summary crap-analysis CRAP scoring: complexity² × untested-ness, via OpenCover + ReportGenerator Risk Hotspots test-authoring xUnit house conventions: naming, Shouldly, NSubstitute, fixtures, meaningful-vs-ornamental tests test-type-selection The unit → integration → e2e ladder: cheapest type that can observe the behaviour stryker-dotnet Scoped Stryker.NET runs and killed/survived interpretation aspire-integration-testing Integration tests with .NET Aspire fixtures and real dependencies playwright-dotnet-refactor Cleaning Playwright codegen drafts into readable xUnit tests Agents The four agents are the four middle phases of the pipeline; each can also be invoked directly.
Agent Role in the pipeline Skills it loads coverage-gap-finder Builds, tests with coverage, and picks exactly one highest-CRAP method; writes gap-report.md. Diagnoses only — never writes tests. crap-analysis test-author Writes exactly one test file, runs it green, never touches the source under test. Re-invoked as a refactor pass when the reviewer requests changes. test-type-selection, test-authoring mutation-validator Proves the test catches regressions — Stryker.NET when installed, a single manual mutation otherwise. Must leave source code untouched. stryker-dotnet test-reviewer Reviews the test file with deliberately fresh eyes (it receives only the file path, no pipeline context) against the two convention skills. test-authoring, test-type-selection The agents communicate through handoff files in a temporary .claude/add-coverage-work/ directory — see the command page for the full flow.
Requirements CLI tools on PATH: dotnet (.NET 8+), git, gh (authenticated) .NET local tools: dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool (required), dotnet-stryker (optional — enables Stryker mutation testing) Test-project NuGet packages: xunit, Shouldly, NSubstitute, coverlet.collector (Microsoft.Playwright only if an e2e test is warranted) coverage.runsettings at the repo root The command’s Phase 0 checks all of these and offers to set up what’s missing — always with your approval, never silently.
Customization CRAP thresholds (> 30, or 0% coverage with complexity ≥ 5) live in agents/coverage-gap-finder.md — fork the repo to adjust. Framework conventions (xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute) live in skills/test-authoring/SKILL.md — fork and edit if your stack uses NUnit, FluentAssertions, or Moq.
description: A command, four agents, and six skills built around finding and closing the riskiest coverage gap

title: microsoft-extensions-dependency-injection
content:
Organize DI registrations using IServiceCollection extension methods. Group related services into composable Add* methods for clean Program.cs and reusable configuration in tests.
What it covers The cure for the 200-line Program.cs: group registrations into chainable extension methods (AddUserServices(), AddEmailServices()), each returning IServiceCollection, placed next to the feature they register.
Naming conventions — Add{Feature}Services / Configure{Feature} / Use{Feature} (for middleware), in files named {Feature}ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs. Layered composition — AddAppServices() → AddDomainServices() → feature methods. The real payoff: tests — tests reuse the production Add* methods and override only what differs, instead of re-registering everything by hand. Lifetime pitfalls — capturing a scoped service in a singleton, and using scoped services in a BackgroundService without IServiceScopeFactory. Ships with File Contents advanced-patterns.md Testing with DI extensions (WebApplicationFactory, standalone ServiceCollection, Akka.Hosting.TestKit), actor scope management, and conditional/factory/keyed registrations Cross-references Points to microsoft-extensions-configuration for the Options pattern, and to an akka-hosting-actor-patterns skill (from the separate NimblePros dotnet-skills collection, not this marketplace) for the Akka-specific patterns its advanced examples touch on.
description: Clean Program.cs, reusable registrations in tests

title: test-type-selection
content:
Decide which kind of test to write — unit, integration, or end-to-end (Playwright) — for a given behaviour. Prefer the cheapest test type that can actually observe the behaviour. Load this skill before choosing where and how to test a coverage gap.
What it covers A three-rung ladder with one rule: move down a rung only because the behaviour is genuinely unobservable at the current one — never for convenience.
Unit — zero out-of-process dependencies; everything in-process (Blazor component rendering via bunit counts as unit). Integration — the behaviour is the interaction with infrastructure or a realistic composition of services: real database via TestContainers, WebApplicationFactory, message broker. End-to-end — the behaviour only exists in a real browser (JS interop, navigation, downloads); automated with Playwright, in a dedicated tests/<App>.E2eTests/ project that is never silently created. The most practical part is the “signals you chose the wrong level” list: mocks that re-implement collaborator logic mean move down; incidental infrastructure means move up; e2e “for extra confidence” means move up. Most coverage gaps resolve to unit tests, since CRAP scoring targets complex in-process logic.
Cross-references Defers all naming/structure conventions to test-authoring. Loaded by the test-author agent (as its decision procedure) and the test-reviewer agent (which checks the chosen level was right) in the /add-coverage pipeline. For deep integration-test patterns at rung 2, see aspire-integration-testing. Single-file skill.
description: The three-rung decision ladder

title: /design-review command
content:
Compare a design asset (image or PDF) against live Playwright screenshots, produce a prioritized findings report, and optionally create GitHub issues per finding.
/playwright-testing:design-review designs/homepage.png https://localhost:5001 /playwright-testing:design-review designs/checkout.pdf https://staging.example.com/checkout /playwright-testing:design-review designs/hero.png https://localhost:5001 --viewport 1440x900 /playwright-testing:design-review designs/dashboard.png https://localhost:5001 --focus "sidebar" --create-issues Arguments Argument Required Description <design-file> Yes Path to a .png, .jpg, .webp, or .pdf design asset <app-url> Yes URL of the live page to compare against --viewport WxH No Viewport dimensions (default 1280x800) --auth-state <path> No Path to a Playwright storage-state or cookies JSON --focus "<section>" No UI area to weight more heavily in classification --create-issues No Create one GitHub issue per design:critical / design:high finding; prompts before lower severities The pipeline Phase What happens 0. Prerequisites Verifies dotnet; confirms design file exists; checks gh auth when --create-issues is set 1. Prepare design reference Copies image or extracts PDF pages to .claude/design-review-work/design-page-*.png 2. Capture screenshots Navigates to the URL with Playwright at the specified viewport; waits for networkidle; saves impl-page-*.png 3. Visual comparison Resizes and diffs each pair; produces annotated diff overlays and per-region crops 4. Classify and prioritize Assigns design:critical → design:info severity per finding 5. Generate report Populates the findings-report template; prints the summary table and top findings to the terminal 6. Create issues (optional) Searches for duplicates first; creates issues for critical/high findings; prompts for lower severities Severity model Label Criteria design:critical Layout broken, content obscured, inaccessible element design:high Wrong component, wrong brand color or typography design:medium Spacing off >8px, missing icon, text truncation design:low Minor shade variation, pixel shadow, icon size ±2px design:info Ambiguous region, dynamic content, out-of-scope variant What it leans on Built on the playwright-design-review skill. That skill defines the severity model, the PDF extraction steps, and the findings-report and GitHub-issue templates. This command applies the full pipeline automatically from a single invocation.
Handoff files All artifacts are written to .claude/design-review-work/ and kept after the run as an audit trail:
Pattern Contents design-page-<N>.png Extracted design reference page(s) impl-page-<N>.png Playwright screenshot(s) diff-overlay-<N>-<M>.png Annotated diff overlay per region design-crop-<N>-<M>.png / impl-crop-<N>-<M>.png Cropped evidence pairs per finding findings-report.md Prioritized findings with summary table issue-<finding-id>.md Per-finding GitHub issue body (when --create-issues is set)
description: Full design-QA pipeline from asset to report, with optional GitHub issue creation

title: opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation
content:
Provides guidance for implementing OpenTelemetry instrumentation in .NET codebases, covering tracing (Activities/Spans), metrics, naming conventions, error handling, performance, and API design best practices.
What it covers Two load-bearing principles: instrumentation must be resilient (an instrumentation exception must never affect application processing; Activity may always be null) and telemetry is public API (emitted span names, tag names, and metrics are subject to the same breaking-change discipline as your code).
Tracing — use ActivitySource (not DiagnosticSource), guard with HasListeners() as the zero-allocation fast path, check IsAllDataRequested before computing expensive tags, and keep runtime data out of operation names (put specifics in DisplayName). Metrics — group instruments in a per-feature Meter class; name recording methods after the outcome (OrderProcessingSucceeded) rather than the mechanism (RecordX); one method per outcome instead of boolean flags; treat high-cardinality dimensions as opt-in to avoid cardinality explosion. Performance rules — Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()/GetElapsedTime() instead of Stopwatch.StartNew(), the TagList struct, no LINQ or string interpolation on hot paths. Testing — assert span parentage and literal span/tag names so telemetry changes are caught like any other breaking change. Cross-references Standalone single-file skill; no supporting files and no references to other skills or agents. Assumes the OpenTelemetry .NET SDK and links out to the OTel semantic conventions. The observability concerns here complement the aspire-integration-testing skill in dotnet-testing, which tests apps whose telemetry this skill helps you emit.
description: ActivitySource, Meter, and telemetry-as-public-API

title: pr
content:
Full lifecycle for creating a pull request, from investigation through deployment verification. Use when the user says “create PR”, “make PR”, “open PR”, “ship this”, or invokes /pr.
Invoke with /workflow:pr.
What it covers Four phases:
Gather context — confirm the target branch (default main), extract work item IDs from the branch name, review git log and git diff --stat against the target. Validate — git fetch origin main and merge origin/main into the branch. A hard rule: always merge, never rebase (rebase breaks build-tag traceability). Create — gh pr create with a body from the shipped template and a conventional-commit title capped at 65 characters. Verify — open the PR in the browser to confirm. Standing rules: keep descriptions factual, always link work items, and never force-push or push to main without explicit confirmation.
Ships with File Contents references/pr-template.md The PR body template (Description, Related Issues, Checklist, Notes for Reviewers) and a copy-paste gh pr create invocation Cross-references Title format comes from conventional-commit; the review skill checks the same 65-character conventional-title rule from the reviewing side. This skill differs from the pr-agent on purpose: the agent is the end of the spec pipeline and always opens a draft PR after verifying acceptance criteria, while /workflow:pr is the interactive path for shipping whatever branch you’re on. Requires git and an authenticated gh.
description: /workflow:pr — context, validation, templated creation, verification

title: stryker-dotnet
content:
Run Stryker.NET mutation testing against a specific .NET source file. Covers installation (local tool), scoped invocation, JSON output parsing, and interpreting killed/survived results to decide pass/fail.
Invoke standalone with /dotnet-testing:mutation-test <source-file-or-class-name>.
What it covers Mutation-testing mechanics — the five mutant statuses (Killed, Survived, NoCoverage, Timeout, CompileError) and the score formula Killed / (Killed + Survived + Timeout) × 100 — but its practical core is scoped invocation: run from the test project directory with --mutate "**/TargetClass.cs" and --test-case-filter, collapsing a multi-minute full-suite run into seconds. It documents the JSON report shape, ready-to-paste parsing snippets, and a pass/fail rubric: ≥ 80% score passes; below 80%, any survived mutant, or zero mutants generated (a scoping problem) fails.
Installation is a pinned local tool (dotnet-stryker in .config/dotnet-tools.json with rollForward: false), with a detection snippet and instructions for falling back to a manual mutation when Stryker isn’t available.
Cross-references The knowledge behind Phase 3 of /add-coverage — the mutation-validator agent loads it and implements both the Stryker path and the manual-mutation fallback the skill describes. Complements crap-analysis: CRAP finds code that lacks tests; mutation testing proves the tests you add actually catch regressions. Single-file skill.
description: Prove a test suite has teeth, in seconds not minutes

title: testing
content:
Playwright-focused testing practice. Most content is stack-neutral; the /playwright-testing:refactor-tests command is .NET-specific.
claude plugin install testing@nimblepros Commands Command Arguments One-line summary /playwright-testing:repro-issue <issue-number-or-url> Fetch a GitHub issue, build a Playwright repro, collect artifacts, and post an evidence comment /playwright-testing:refactor-tests <file-or-glob> Upgrade Playwright .NET tests to semantic locators and intent-based assertions, confirmed green /playwright-testing:design-review <design-file> <url> [options] Diff a design asset against live Playwright screenshots and produce a prioritized findings report Skills Skill One-line summary playwright-issue-repro-report Turn a GitHub bug report into a Playwright repro with screenshot/video/trace evidence and a structured issue comment playwright-design-review Compare a design asset (image or PDF) against live Playwright screenshots, classify differences by severity, and optionally create GitHub issues per finding Agents e2e-tester writes, runs, and debugs end-to-end suites across Playwright, Cypress, and Selenium. It follows a discover → design → implement → validate → report loop, with a resilient selector priority (data-testid → ARIA roles → visible text → CSS as last resort), and handles the messy edge cases: flaky tests, CI-only failures, auth bypass via API or stored state, and database seeding. It keeps project-scoped memory of framework versions, fixtures, known flaky tests, and selector conventions across sessions.
The agent and skills are independent — the agent doesn’t load any skill — but they pair naturally: e2e-tester builds and maintains suites, while playwright-issue-repro-report turns individual bug reports into evidence and playwright-design-review audits implementations against design assets.
Related plugins If your stack is .NET, install dotnet-testing as well — it carries the xUnit conventions, coverage analysis, and mutation testing that this plugin deliberately leaves out. Its playwright-dotnet-refactor skill is the .NET-specific complement to the Playwright practice here; the /playwright-testing:refactor-tests command in this plugin applies that skill in batch over a file or glob.
description: Three commands, two skills, and one agent for Playwright-based testing and QA

title: architecture
content:
Architecture decisions and the documentation that records them. Language-agnostic by design — architecture philosophy does not live inside a language plugin.
claude plugin install architecture@nimblepros Commands Command One-line summary /architecture:adr Draft, review, and register a new ADR for a design or technology decision Skills Skill One-line summary adr-writing The full ADR authoring workflow: naming, numbering, required sections, status lifecycle, and resolving duplicate numbers from parallel branches Agents technical-writer creates and reviews technical documentation — API docs, READMEs, guides, tutorials, ADRs, changelogs — for clarity, accuracy, and consistency. It follows a review-code-change → update-docs → lint → verify workflow with an explicit quality checklist, and keeps project-scoped memory of a project’s documentation conventions and terminology across sessions. Its worked examples assume a Hugo documentation site (Geekdoc theme) and a CLI project; adapt the paths and commands to your own documentation tooling.
The agent and skill are independent — technical-writer does not load adr-writing — but they cover the same territory from two directions: the skill defines what a good ADR is, and the agent is a general documentation workhorse that can produce one.
Roadmap Candidates for this plugin as content is written: modular-monolith, vertical-slice, clean-architecture, architecture-review, and a dependency-analyzer agent.
Seen in the wild This repository practices what the plugin preaches: the marketplace restructure is recorded in ADR 0001, written in the format this skill defines.
description: ADR writing and the documentation that records decisions

title: aspire-integration-testing
content:
Write integration tests using .NET Aspire’s testing facilities with xUnit. Covers test fixtures, distributed application setup, endpoint discovery, and patterns for testing ASP.NET Core apps with real dependencies.
What it covers Six core principles: real dependencies over mocks, dynamic port binding, IAsyncLifetime fixture lifecycle, runtime endpoint discovery (never hard-coded URLs), xUnit collections for parallel isolation, and always waiting on health checks before running tests.
The canonical pattern is an AspireAppFixture built with DistributedApplicationTestingBuilder, with explicit startup and health timeouts, shared across a test collection. The skill also flags a non-obvious gotcha: disabling config-reload-on-change via a [ModuleInitializer], because each test host’s file watcher otherwise exhausts Linux inotify limits in CI. A troubleshooting table covers timeouts, port conflicts, flaky timing, and dynamic connection strings.
Ships with File Contents advanced-patterns.md Endpoint-discovery helpers, database testing with Respawn resets, an Aspire + Playwright combined fixture, conditional resource configuration, test-auth and fake-external-service patterns, message-queue tests ci-and-tooling.md GitHub Actions workflow, resource-readiness retry loops, and Aspire CLI + MCP integration so Claude can query live resource state Cross-references This is reference material (not slash-invocable, and not part of the /add-coverage pipeline) — Claude loads it when writing integration tests, i.e. rung 2 of the test-type-selection ladder. External dependencies: Aspire.Hosting.Testing, Docker, and optionally Respawn, TestContainers-style resources, and the Aspire CLI.
description: Real databases, real services, dynamic ports, health-checked fixtures

title: review
content:
Review code changes using parallel agents. Works on local diffs or open PRs. Checks project conventions, scans for bugs, verifies claims, and resolves review threads. Use when the user says “review”, “review this”, “review PR”, “check this PR”, or invokes /review.
Invoke with /workflow:review, optionally passing a PR number. Without one it reviews the local diff against origin/main — a PR is not required, and the skill explicitly forbids creating one just to run a review.
What it covers A five-step fan-out review:
Pick the target — a PR (via gh pr view / gh pr diff) or the local diff. Dispatch five independent agents over the same diff: Bug Scan (logic errors only — style and type errors are CI’s job), Git History Context (is the change consistent with the file’s evolution?), Shared Code Impact (all callers of every modified file — called out as “the #1 cause of errors that make it into production”), Project Convention Check (branch naming, conventional PR title under 65 chars), and Security and Secrets Check (hardcoded secrets, OWASP Top 10, authn/authz changes). Score every finding 0–100 for confidence — only findings scoring 75+ are reported, because “false positives erode trust in the review process.” Report in a fixed format with evidence and file/line links. PR only: list unresolved review threads via the GitHub GraphQL API and resolve the ones that are verifiably fixed — never on assumption. Cross-references This is the “independent review by a separate agent” phase that implement-feature requires before opening a PR. Its convention check enforces the same title rules as pr and conventional-commit. It reads the project’s CLAUDE.md — conventions stated there count as high-confidence findings. Requires git and an authenticated gh (including gh api graphql for thread resolution). No supporting files.
description: /workflow:review — five independent review lenses over one diff

title: playwright-dotnet-refactor
content:
Refactor generated Playwright .NET test drafts into readable xUnit tests with role-based locators, intent-based assertions, and minimal helper extraction. Use when a generated Playwright test is noisy, brittle, or hard to maintain and needs cleanup without changing user intent.
What it covers A cleanup pass for Playwright codegen output, governed by six rules:
Preserve user intent exactly — no silently added or removed scenario steps. Semantic locators in strict priority order: GetByRole → GetByLabel/GetByPlaceholder → GetByText → GetByTestId; avoid CSS/XPath. Readable xUnit with obvious Arrange-Act-Assert. Extract helpers only when readability genuinely improves. Assert only user-observable behaviour — never internal IDs or CSS internals. Deterministic waits via Playwright assertions — no arbitrary sleeps. The output contract requires a rationale alongside the refactored code: what locators changed, what assertions changed, what was extracted, and what was assumed.
Ships with File Contents assets/refactor-prompt-template.md A reusable prompt with slots for scenario intent, the generated draft, and constraints Cross-references Standalone — not wired into the /add-coverage pipeline. It shares Playwright ground with the stack-neutral playwright-issue-repro-report skill in the testing plugin: that one produces repro tests from bug reports; this one cleans up generated tests into maintainable xUnit.
description: From codegen noise to intent-revealing tests

title: workflow
content:
The issue → spec → implementation → review → PR loop, driven through the gh CLI.
claude plugin install workflow@nimblepros Two ways through the loop This plugin offers the same journey at two granularities:
The agent pipeline — issue-agent breaks an issue into subtasks → spec-agent writes a spec to .claude/specs/ using the feature-specification skill → you (or another agent) implement → review checks the result → pr-agent opens a draft PR. The single-skill path — implement-feature collapses the middle of that loop into one workflow: gather full issue context, persist a phased plan in .claude/plans/, implement, get an independent agent review, verify, open a PR. Skills Skill Invoke One-line summary feature-specification — The structured spec format written to .claude/specs/, with phased checklists and verifiable “Done When” criteria implement-feature /workflow:implement The end-to-end issue workflow: context → plan → implement → independent review → verify → PR commit /workflow:commit Conversation-aware commit messages following Conventional Commits pr /workflow:pr Full PR lifecycle: context, merge-from-main validation, templated gh pr create, verification review /workflow:review Five parallel review agents over a local diff or PR, with confidence-scored findings Reference Page What it is conventional-commit The Conventional Commits format reference: type taxonomy, scope, SemVer impact, and the PR-title format. Not an installable skill — loaded by commit and cited by pr-agent and the pr skill. Agents Agent Purpose issue-agent Reads backlog items with gh issue view, decomposes them into - [ ] checklists written back to the issue, creates linked sub-issues, and hands scope off to spec-agent. spec-agent Turns a GitHub issue into an implementation-ready spec in .claude/specs/, delegating document structure to the feature-specification skill. pr-agent The terminal gate: runs build and tests, confirms every acceptance criterion in both the spec and the issue checklist, then opens a draft PR (using the conventional-commit title format) and leaves it draft for developer review. Where files land Two persistence directories, easy to confuse:
.claude/specs/<issue-number>-<short-title>.md — specs, from spec-agent / feature-specification .claude/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-issue-NNN-short-slug.md — implementation plans, from implement-feature Requirements git gh (GitHub CLI, authenticated — run gh auth login) Some skills carry .NET-flavored examples (build/test verification commands), but the workflow itself is language-agnostic — substitute your own build and test commands.
description: The issue → spec → implementation → review → PR loop

title: NimblePros Claude Plugins
content:
Welcome to the NimblePros Claude Plugins documentation. This site explains what each plugin in the marketplace provides, how the skills, agents, and commands inside each plugin work together, and how to install only the parts you want.
What is this marketplace? NimblePros/claude-plugins is a Claude Code plugin marketplace: a single repository you add once, after which you can install any of its five plugins independently. Each plugin bundles related skills (reference knowledge Claude loads on demand), agents (specialized subagents for focused tasks), and — where it makes sense — commands (slash commands that orchestrate multi-step pipelines).
claude plugin marketplace add NimblePros/claude-plugins claude plugin install dotnet-testing@nimblepros The five plugins Plugin What you get dotnet C#/.NET practice: coding standards, package management, Options/DI patterns, OpenTelemetry, NuGet publishing dotnet-testing The /dotnet-testing:add-coverage pipeline, CRAP analysis, Stryker.NET mutation testing, xUnit conventions, Aspire integration testing testing Stack-neutral testing: end-to-end test authoring, Playwright issue-repro reports architecture ADR writing and technical documentation workflow Issue → spec → implementation → review → PR, over the gh CLI How the plugins are organized Content is grouped by capability, not by artifact type — skills, agents, and commands that work together ship together. Two principles shape the split:
Language-specific vs. stack-neutral. The dotnet and dotnet-testing plugins assume the .NET toolchain; testing, architecture, and workflow do not. That is why testing exists twice: dotnet-testing carries everything that depends on dotnet test, xUnit, and Stryker.NET, while testing carries Playwright/e2e practice that works on any stack. Self-contained plugins. A skill ships in the same plugin as any agent or command that loads it. No plugin depends on another being installed. The rationale for this structure is recorded in ADR 0001.
Sections Getting Started — install options, namespacing, and migration from the old single plugin dotnet, dotnet-testing, testing, architecture, workflow — one section per plugin, with a summary page per skill
